二胡屬弦鳴樂器，常見於中國傳統與當代音樂場合：可作獨奏，也用於小型合奏、江南絲竹: The erhu is a chordophone, heard in both traditional and contemporary Chinese music: as a solo instrument, in small ensembles, in Jiangnan sizhu, in opera and drama orchestras and in the modern large Chinese orchestra. Solo pieces such as Liu Tianhua's 《月夜》 (“Moonlit Night”) and 《燭影搖紅》 (“Candle Shadows Flickering Red”), Hua Yanjun's 《二泉映月》 (“Moon Reflected on the Second Spring”), Huang Haihuai's 《賽馬》 (“Horse Racing”), Liu Mingyuan's 《河南小曲》 (“Henan Ditty”) and Liu Wenjin's 《三門峽暢想曲》 (“Sanmenxia Capriccio”) can mostly be accompanied by the yangqin. Today it also appears in pop, rock and jazz arrangements, in Cirque du Soleil's show 《O》, on Shen Yun tours, in fusion progressive rock, in Taiwanese black metal and in the song 《Field Below》.
二胡屬胡琴家族，可追溯至唐代出現於中國的奚琴，奚人樂器；宋代演變，中華民國時期改: The erhu belongs to the huqin family and can be traced to the xiqin, an instrument of the Xi people that appeared in China in the Tang dynasty; it changed form in the Song, and was renamed erhu in the Republican period. It was at first mostly a folk instrument of the south, while the north preferred the sihu; in the 1920s Liu Tianhua brought it to Beijing and combined European music theory with violin technique, tuning it to d and a and composing solos, which drove its modernisation. In the same period Zhou Shaomei, Zhou Ronggen and Tao Hongmao improved the neck, the soundbox, the python skin, the soft bow and the thick strings. Professional national orchestras appeared in the 1950s and 60s and increased the demand; in 1963 the first national erhu competition was held at the Shanghai Spring Music Festival. In the 1970s Tang Liangde, Wang Guotong and Man Ruixing improved the design and developed the erquan qin.
二胡為弦鳴樂器，發聲以弓毛夾於兩弦間摩擦，使蟒蛇皮振動產生音色；因無指板，按弦時: The erhu is a chordophone: the hair of the bow is threaded between the two strings and rubbed, making the python skin vibrate and producing the timbre; because there is no fretboard, the fingertip only presses the string and does not touch the neck. Modern practice tunes it in perfect fifths, the inner string lower and the outer higher, and the usual range is about two and a half octaves, at most three and a half. Volume and timbre are affected by the thickness and tightness of the snakeskin and by the thickness and outline of the soundbox, and the screw on the bow adjusts the tension of the hair. Within the huqin family the erhu occupies the upper-middle register, and in the modern Chinese orchestra its pitch is second only to the gaohu.

The erhu is a Chinese two-string bowed instrument of the huqin family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.313, classified as a chordophone. It is built from a neck, a soundbox, two strings, a qianjin (nut), a bridge and a bow; the front of the soundbox is covered with python skin, the bow hair passes between the inner and outer strings, there is no fretboard, and the left hand stops the strings without touching the neck. Modern practice mostly tunes it in perfect fifths. The erhu can be used for solo playing, in small ensembles and in the large Chinese orchestra, and it also appears in Jiangnan sizhu, as accompaniment in opera, and in traditional and contemporary pop, rock and jazz line-ups.

演奏二胡時，左手持琴按弦，右手拉弓，弓毛置於內外兩弦之間拉奏。初學可先採坐姿，若: To play the erhu, the left hand holds the instrument and stops the strings while the right hand bows, with the bow hair threaded between the inner and outer strings. A beginner can start seated; for a procession or a performance, a hook can be fitted so that the instrument hangs at the waist and is played standing. The sound comes from the bow hair rubbing the strings, which makes the python skin vibrate; the instrument has no fretboard, so the fingertip presses the string without pressing it down to the neck. The usual modern tuning is d' on the inner string and a' on the outer. Practise in this order: hold the instrument, tune it, bow the open strings, then add whole-bow, long-bow, short-bow, push and pull strokes, and gradually work on vibrato, harmonics and slides.
琴身常用紫檀、紅木、烏木等硬木，亦有雞翅木、血檀、大葉紫檀、非洲紅花梨、非洲紫檀: The body is usually a hardwood such as rosewood, padauk or ebony, and also wenge, bloodwood, large-leaf rosewood, African padauk or African rosewood, or parts chosen for looks rather than sound, such as ivory, jade or plastic. The sounding body, the front of the soundbox, is covered with python skin, for which polyester film is a substitute. The strings were silk in earlier times and are mostly steel today, and the outer layer may be a silver or nickel alloy. The qianjin is made of cotton thread, nylon line, silk or metal. The bridge is maple, ebony, rosewood, padauk, pine knot, bamboo or paper. The pad under the bridge is cloth, fur or latex. The tuning pegs are wooden or metal machine pegs. The sound windows are carved from wood. The bow stick is usually bamboo, sometimes carbon fibre; the hair is mainly white horsehair, and the frog may be white jade, ivory, wood or plastic.
